newsitem.title: POLAND: Poland says law broken in 1949 Swiss bank deal.
newsitem.headline: Poland says law broken in 1949 Swiss bank deal.

text.p: Poland said on Friday that arrangements made under a 1949 deal with Switzerland involving the return of money from Swiss bank accounts of Polish citizens who perished in World War Two had broken the law.

Switzerland has been accused of wrongly agreeing to give money to Poland from unclaimed bank accounts of Polish Jews killed in the Holocaust as part of accords to compensate Swiss citizens whose assets were seized in communist Poland.

The Polish Foreign Ministry said it had studied documents involved in the deal and would call an inter-ministerial committee of experts to clarify the issue quickly and find out how much money was involved.
"The Foreign Ministry considers that the method agreed in these agreements for allocating accounts of Polish citizens ...did not conform with the law," its statement said.

It said the deal did not require lists of names of Polish account holders to be submitted and there was no guarantee that proper procedures for the Polish treasury to take over heirless legacies would be applied.

The ministry said Poland and Switzerland signed agreements on June 25, 1949, on commodities exchanges -- largely sales of Polish coal -- and on compensation for Swiss citizens. Both had confidential protocols.
The compensation accord had a protocol and exchange of letters on unclaimed accounts of Poles in Swiss institutions.
A common payments mechanism, an account "N" in Switzerland belonging to the National Bank of Poland (NBP), was set up for these arrangements, the ministry said.

"This account took some of the money from Polish exports and distributed it to Swiss citizens who had claims after their property was nationalised," ministry spokesman Pawel Dobrowolski told Reuters. "At the same time money from Polish accounts held in Swiss banks was flowing the other way into it."
He added: "You have the unusual situation of private and public funds existing in the same account, which is really breaking the law."

The ministry statement said the experts' committee would try to throw light on the whole problem, "especially to obtain full information on the size of the financial flows through account "N" for the so-called dead-hand accounts."

Some Swiss commentators have argued that the agreement on the dormant accounts was openly discussed at the time and reflected international private law that says heirless assets belong to the state where the owner last lived.
Asked whether former owners or their heirs could still claim money from these accounts, Dobrowolski said this was unclear and one of the issues the experts would examine.
"We simply don"t have any papers or materials after 1949 -- some other institutions may have," he added.
